Dear Ledgerly Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the UX Researcher II role on the AI Assistant. For the past four years I've been a product data analyst at Cadence, a consumer fitness app. More and more, my work there has come down to the questions this role is built around: how do people experience AI features that act on their personal data, and how do we know if those features are actually working for them?

The clearest example is AI Coach, which adjusts users' workout plans based on their activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. I owned the analysis of its four-week launch test with about 180,000 users. Weekly workouts rose 8.0% (95% CI 6.1–9.9%) and 7-day retention rose 2.1 points. I checked each week for a novelty effect, and the lift was still there in week four. After launch, I helped build the coding scheme for about 1,200 open-ended survey responses. The headline number was 72% positive. The finding I kept coming back to didn't fit any sentiment bucket, though: users who didn't understand why their plan had changed. I pushed to report it separately. To me it shows why satisfaction scores alone can miss whether people understand and trust what an AI is doing. That gap matters even more when the AI is moving someone's money, and building metrics that capture it is the part of this role I'm most excited about.

I bring strong quantitative skills. I run the analysis for about 20 A/B tests a year: analysis plans, power calculations, and readouts. I've also argued for rigor when it mattered. I talked a PM out of an underpowered one-week test and into a three-week test with a pre-registered primary metric. When I found a sample ratio mismatch in an onboarding test, I traced it to a redirect bug and recommended a rerun instead of reweighting the data. I also rebuilt our leadership dashboard from 23 tiles down to 9, so the weekly review focuses on the metrics that drive decisions.

My qualitative experience is newer. I took notes for the UX research team's interviews on AI Coach, and I ran an interview study with affinity mapping in my HCI coursework. That work is why I'm moving toward research. I want to own studies end to end, and I think analysts who know experiment data well can help make qualitative findings hard to ignore.

I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I could contribute to Ledgerly's AI Assistant.

Best,
Riley Nakamura

**Statement of Purpose**
Riley Nakamura · PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Northeastern University · Fall 2027

In July 2025, I was coding about 1,200 open-ended survey responses about AI Coach, a feature at Cadence, the consumer fitness app where I work as a product data analyst. AI Coach changes users' workout plans based on their activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. By the measures we had planned, it worked. I analyzed its four-week launch test with about 180,000 users and found an 8% increase in weekly workouts and a 2.1-point lift in 7-day retention. But one group of responses didn't fit our coding scheme. These users weren't positive or negative about the feature; they were confused. They didn't understand why their plan had changed. The experiment showed that people worked out more. It couldn't show whether they understood what the system was doing for them, or agreed with it. That gap is what I want to study in a PhD.

**Research interests**

AI features that quietly adapt based on personal data are now common. They show up in fitness, health, and personal finance products. I want to understand how people make sense of these systems when they change something, and how that understanding affects trust, reliance, and long-term use. Three questions interest me most:

1. **How do people explain adaptive changes to themselves?** When a system changes a plan, a budget, or a recommendation without saying why, people form their own theories about what happened. I want to know what those theories look like, when they're accurate, and when a wrong theory leads people to over-trust or abandon the system.
2. **How can we measure understanding alongside behavior?** My work has shown me that engagement can rise while understanding stays low, and standard experiment metrics won't catch it. I'm interested in measures of user understanding and well-calibrated trust that can sit next to behavioral outcomes in field experiments.
3. **How do the stakes change things?** A confusing change to a workout plan is an annoyance. A confusing change to someone's savings or medication reminders is not. I want to study whether people need different explanations, and different amounts of control, as the stakes rise.

These questions are still loose, and I expect them to sharpen through coursework and work with faculty.

**What I bring**

For four years at Cadence, I've owned the analysis for about 20 A/B tests a year: analysis plans, power calculations, and readouts. That work has made me careful about measurement, because I've seen how measurement choices shape what a team believes. When I found a 52/48 traffic split in an onboarding test, I confirmed the sample ratio mismatch, traced it to a redirect bug that dropped some Android users, and argued for rerunning the test instead of reweighting the data. When a PM proposed a one-week test that couldn't detect the effect we cared about, I negotiated a longer test with a pre-registered primary metric. For ratio metrics, I implemented user-level bootstrap confidence intervals and checked them against the delta method. On AI Coach, I checked week by week for a novelty effect before we trusted the lift. These experiences taught me to ask what a number can and can't support, and I want to bring that habit to research on human-AI interaction.

My qualitative training is less developed, and it's the part I most want to build. As an undergraduate in Information Science (HCI track), I ran a semi-structured interview study with six students, synthesized it with affinity diagramming, and ran a usability test with eight participants for my capstone. At Cadence, I volunteered to take notes for four interviews that our UX research team ran on AI Coach. I worked out a note format that kept timestamped quotes and kept what we observed separate from how we interpreted it. Watching the researcher's follow-up questions uncover reasons that no survey item had captured was the most interesting part of my job that year. That experience convinced me that the questions I care about need both methods: experiments to show what people do, and interviews and diary studies to show why.

I haven't published or led an independent research study yet. A PhD is where I want to learn to do that well.

**Why a PhD, and why Khoury**

In industry, research questions are scoped to a launch decision. The responses about not understanding plan changes ended up in an appendix because they didn't change whether AI Coach shipped. That was a reasonable call for the product, but the underlying question applies across products and domains, and it deserves sustained study rather than a footnote. I want the training to study it rigorously and publish findings that shape how adaptive AI products are designed and evaluated.

**Statement of Purpose**
Riley Nakamura · PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Northeastern University · Fall 2027

In the summer of 2025, I was helping code about 1,200 open-ended survey responses about AI Coach, a feature at Cadence, the fitness app where I work as a data analyst. AI Coach changes your workout plan based on your activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. By the numbers, the launch went well: people in the test worked out about 8% more each week. But in the written responses, maybe one in ten people said something that didn't fit that picture. Their plan had changed and they had no idea why. Some asked how the app knew they'd slept badly. A couple had turned off health-data sharing.

In the final deck, all of it was folded into a single "72% positive." I understood why. The team needed a number to make a launch decision. But the +8% and what people actually wrote felt like two different products. The first showed that the feature changed what people did. The second showed that many of them couldn't tell what it was doing, or why it seemed to know so much about them.

A few months later, I took notes for interviews our UX research team ran about AI Coach. There wasn't one dramatic quote. What stayed with me was hearing people explain, in their own words, what they thought the app was doing with their data. Their explanations were specific, sometimes wrong, and clearly shaped how they felt about using it. Hearing those explanations was the best part of my month.

That's the question I want to study: **what do people think is going on when an app uses their own data to decide things for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say?**

More and more everyday products work this way. Fitness apps adjust your training, finance apps move your money, and health apps decide what to remind you about. Usually they don't explain themselves, so people form their own understanding of what the system knows and why it acts. I want to study what that understanding looks like and where it comes from. I also want to find out what kinds of explanation, control, or ability to push back make people feel like participants rather than subjects. Privacy is part of this. Sometimes the question really is "how did it know that?" But it's not the whole picture. People who are fine with sharing their data may still want to understand and shape what's done with it.

My path to this question has run through measurement. For four years, I've analyzed experiments and built the metrics my team uses to judge features. That work taught me to be careful about what a number can actually support. It also showed me what numbers leave out. I don't want to study how to make people engage more. I want to understand the people behind the engagement numbers. My research experience so far is modest: an interview study with affinity mapping and a usability test from my undergraduate HCI coursework, plus the interviews I sat in on at Cadence. I haven't published or led my own study. I'm applying because I want to learn to do this research well. That means combining interviews, diary studies, and surveys with the experimental work I already know, so that what people say about these systems is taken as seriously as what they do.

I'm especially interested in working with Professor Tianshi Li. Her research on how AI autonomy and personalization affect people's sense of control, and on the mental models people form about AI systems that handle their personal data, is close to the questions I want to pursue. [**Add one or two more faculty after you check them.**]

What I took from AI Coach is that a feature can succeed by every measure we track while many of its users don't know what it's doing to them. I want to spend the next several years understanding that gap, and helping design systems that close it.
